idiom_name: Future { } on an ExecutionContext + Future.sequence/Await aggregation
implementation_notes: scala.concurrent.Future is the master's dispatch: Future { computePart(i) } starts a sub-task on the implicit ExecutionContext and returns immediately, Future.sequence or traverse (or a for-comprehension) joins, and Await.result blocks the calling thread for the final value. ExecutionContext.global is backed by a work-stealing ForkJoinPool sized to the available processors; long blocking calls inside a Future need blocking { } (ForkJoinPool.managedBlock) or, better, a dedicated ExecutionContext from ExecutionContext.fromExecutor, because the global pool compensates only for notified blocking and can otherwise starve. Failures are observable through onComplete/recover or at Await, and scala.concurrent.Future has no cancellation - when the master must cancel siblings, Pekko/Akka actors, ZIO or Cats-Effect fibers are the library answer. Parallel collections (par) are the data-parallel cousin for uniform elementwise work.
code_sketch:
implicit val ec: ExecutionContext = ExecutionContext.global
val parts: Seq[Future[Double]] =
  (0 until n).map(i => Future { computePart(i) })          // identical workers
val total: Double =
  Await.result(Future.sequence(parts).map(_.sum), Duration.Inf)  // join + combine
pitfalls: Blocking inside a Future on the global pool starves it (the pool can grow to thousands of threads); wrap blocking calls in blocking { } or use a dedicated ExecutionContext.
Future has no cancellation and starts eagerly, so a failed or abandoned sub-task cannot be stopped - only ignored (or the whole design moves to actors/fibers).
Await inside the same bounded pool deadlocks: never block on a future from a thread that the pool needs to complete it.
Side effects in parallel collections and unordered traversals are non-deterministic; keep the combine associative and pure (the parallel-collections guide documents this explicitly).
